title: Fraction-Percentage Equivalence Table
summary: Memorize the standard fraction-to-percentage table so you can convert instantly without division during DI and simplification questions.
body:
Speed in Data Interpretation and Simplification comes from recognizing common fractions as percentages on sight, instead of dividing every time. Memorize this table cold:

| Fraction | Percentage |
|---|---|
| 1/2 | 50% |
| 1/3 | 33.33% |
| 1/4 | 25% |
| 1/5 | 20% |
| 1/6 | 16.67% |
| 1/7 | 14.28% |
| 1/8 | 12.5% |
| 1/9 | 11.11% |
| 1/10 | 10% |
| 1/11 | 9.09% |
| 1/12 | 8.33% |

**How to use it:** Whenever a question asks for a percentage of a number, first check if it hides one of these fractions. Finding 33.33% of 96 by long multiplication wastes time; recognizing that 33.33% = 1/3 lets you just divide 96 by 3.

**Worked example:** What is 16.67% of 420?
Recognize 16.67% = 1/6. So the answer is 420 / 6 = 70, found in seconds instead of multiplying 420 by 0.1667.

Extend the same habit to multiples: 66.67% = 2/3, 37.5% = 3/8, 62.5% = 5/8. Once this table is automatic, DI questions with percentage-based options stop needing a calculator-style approach — you simply match the fraction pattern and divide.

title: Alligation Cross Method
summary: Use the alligation cross to find mixture ratios instantly by cross-subtracting from the mean value, without setting up equations.
body:
The rule of alligation lets you find the ratio in which two ingredients of different values (price, concentration, speed, and so on) must be mixed to get a desired mean value — without writing a single equation.

**The cross method:** Write the cheaper/lower value (C1) and the dearer/higher value (C2) side by side, with the mean value (M) placed between them. Then cross-subtract diagonally: the difference (C2 - M) becomes C1's share of the ratio, and the difference (M - C1) becomes C2's share.

| Side | Cross-difference gives |
|---|---|
| C1 (cheaper) | C2 - M |
| C2 (dearer) | M - C1 |

Ratio of C1 : C2 = (C2 - M) : (M - C1).

**Worked example:** A shopkeeper mixes tea worth Rs 40/kg with tea worth Rs 60/kg to get a mixture worth Rs 45/kg. Find the ratio.
C1 = 40, C2 = 60, M = 45.
Ratio = (60-45) : (45-40) = 15 : 5 = 3 : 1.
So for every 3 kg of the Rs 40 tea, use 1 kg of the Rs 60 tea.

This same cross works for mixing milk-water solutions, blending speeds in average-speed problems, and even average-marks or average-age questions where one group's value differs from another's. Whenever you see two source values and one resulting average, reach for the cross instead of algebra.

title: CI-SI Two-Year Difference Shortcut
summary: For a two-year period, the difference between compound interest and simple interest equals principal times the square of the rate, giving a one-step formula.
body:
For exactly **2 years**, there is a direct shortcut connecting CI and SI so you never need to calculate both in full.

**The formula:**
CI - SI (for 2 years) = P x (R/100)^2

This works because the only difference between CI and SI over two years is that CI earns 'interest on the first year's interest,' while SI does not. That extra amount is simply the first year's interest earned again at rate R.

**Worked example:** Find the difference between CI and SI on Rs 5,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum.
Difference = P x (R/100)^2 = 5000 x (10/100)^2 = 5000 x 0.01 = Rs 50.

Check: SI = (5000 x 10 x 2)/100 = Rs 1000. CI = 5000 x (1.1^2 - 1) = 5000 x 0.21 = Rs 1050. Difference = 1050 - 1000 = Rs 50. Matches instantly.

**Bonus for 3 years:** Difference = P x (R/100)^2 x (3 + R/100).

Whenever a question gives you the CI-SI difference for 2 years and asks for the principal or the rate, plug straight into P x (R/100)^2 = difference and solve for the missing variable — this avoids expanding the full compound interest formula altogether.

title: Quadratic Roots Sign-Pattern Method
summary: Read the signs of b and c in ax^2+bx+c to predict whether both roots are positive, negative, or of opposite sign, without solving the equation.
body:
In SBI PO quant, most quadratic-equation questions only ask you to compare the roots of two equations (greater, smaller, equal, or no relation) — you rarely need the exact roots. The sign pattern of b and c tells you the sign of the roots instantly, using the relations **sum of roots = -b/a** and **product of roots = c/a**.

| Sign of c (= product) | Sign of -b (= sum) | Roots |
|---|---|---|
| Positive | Negative | Both roots negative |
| Positive | Positive | Both roots positive |
| Negative | Either | One root positive, one negative |

**Worked example:** x^2 - 7x + 12 = 0
c = 12 (positive), sum = -b = 7 (positive) -> both roots positive. Indeed, factoring gives (x-3)(x-4) = 0, roots 3 and 4 — both positive, confirming the pattern.

**Using it for comparison questions:** If equation I gives 'both roots positive' and equation II gives 'both roots negative,' you can immediately conclude every root of equation I is greater than every root of equation II, without computing a single value. Save the actual factoring for when the sign pattern alone does not resolve the comparison, such as when both equations give same-sign roots and you need exact magnitude.

title: Number Series Pattern Checklist
summary: Run through a fixed checklist of pattern types in order — differences, ratios, squares/cubes, mixed operations — to identify a series pattern within seconds.
body:
Instead of staring blankly at a series, run through this checklist top to bottom; one of these covers almost every SBI PO series:

1. **Constant difference** (AP): 5, 10, 15, 20 -> add 5 each time.
2. **Constant ratio** (GP): 3, 6, 12, 24 -> multiply by 2 each time.
3. **Increasing/decreasing difference**: 2, 3, 5, 8, 12 -> differences 1, 2, 3, 4.
4. **Squares/cubes with an offset**: 3, 8, 15, 24, 35 -> n^2 - 1 for n = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
5. **Alternating pattern**: two interwoven series; check odd and even positions separately.
6. **Mixed operations**: +2, x2, +2, x2 alternating.
7. **Two-step differences**: the differences themselves form a series.

**Worked example:** 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?
Differences: 4, 6, 8, 10 — increasing by 2 each time (checklist item 3). The next difference is 12, so the answer is 30 + 12 = 42.
(Cross-check with item 4: this is actually n(n+1) for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — both routes agree.)

Always compute the first-level differences before anything else; if they are not constant, take the second-level differences next. Most 'hard' series turn out to be a squares/cubes pattern in disguise, so check item 4 early if plain differences look irregular.

title: DI Approximation Strategy
summary: When answer options are far apart, round the numbers in a DI table before calculating so you compare estimates instead of exact values.
body:
The biggest time-waster in Data Interpretation is calculating exact values when the answer options do not require that precision. Before doing any division or percentage calculation, **scan the five options first**.

**Rule of thumb:**
- If options are far apart (for example, 24%, 31%, 38%, 45%, 52%), round every number to the nearest convenient value and estimate — you will still land closer to one option than any other.
- If options are close together (for example, 24.2%, 24.6%, 25.1%, 25.4%), you must calculate more precisely, but you can still round secondary numbers.

**Worked example:** A table shows a company's profit as Rs 4,87,650 out of revenue Rs 19,34,200. Options: 20%, 25%, 30%, 35%, 40%.
Round to 4,90,000 / 19,50,000, which is close to 49/195, which is close to 1/4 = 25%. Done in seconds, with no long division needed, and it clearly matches the option 25%.

**Extra speed habit:** Round both numerator and denominator in the *same direction proportionally* so the ratio does not drift — rounding revenue down but profit up (or vice versa) can flip your estimate onto the wrong option. When in doubt, round both to two or three significant figures only, never fewer, and always glance at option spacing before picking a rounding level.

title: Time-Work LCM/Efficiency Method
summary: Convert individual completion times into one-day work rates using the LCM as total work, turning time-and-work problems into simple efficiency arithmetic.
body:
Avoid fractions entirely in Time & Work by assuming **total work = LCM of the given times**, then working in whole-number 'efficiency' units per day.

**Method:**
1. Take the LCM of all given completion times as the total units of work.
2. Each person's efficiency (units/day) = Total work divided by their individual time.
3. Combine efficiencies for joint work, then Time = Total work divided by combined efficiency.

**Worked example:** A can finish a job in 12 days, B in 15 days. How long will they take working together?
LCM(12, 15) = 60 units of work.
A's efficiency = 60/12 = 5 units/day. B's efficiency = 60/15 = 4 units/day.
Combined = 9 units/day. Time together = 60/9 = 6.67 days.

**Wage-sharing bonus:** If A and B are paid together for a job, split the wages in the ratio of their efficiencies (5:4 above), not their times — a common trap is dividing wages by time instead of work-rate.

This method also extends cleanly to pipes-and-cisterns (treat an outlet pipe's efficiency as negative) and to problems where efficiency is given as a ratio instead of days — just assign efficiency values directly and skip the LCM step.

title: Successive Percentage Change Formula
summary: Combine two successive percentage changes into one net percentage using a+b+ab/100, with correct signs for increases and decreases.
body:
When a value changes by a%, then by b% (in that order), the **single equivalent net change** is:

Net% = a + b + (a x b)/100

Use **positive** values for increases and **negative** values for decreases. This one formula replaces multiplying two separate multipliers together.

**Worked example 1 (two increases):** Price rises 20%, then rises 10%.
Net% = 20 + 10 + (20 x 10)/100 = 30 + 2 = 32% increase.

**Worked example 2 (increase then decrease):** Salary rises 25%, then falls 20%.
Net% = 25 + (-20) + (25 x -20)/100 = 5 - 5 = 0% — no net change at all, even though 25 and 20 look quite different.

**Worked example 3 (successive discounts):** Two discounts of 10% and 15% on an item.
Net% = -10 + (-15) + (-10 x -15)/100 = -25 + 1.5 = -23.5%, an overall 23.5% discount, not 25%, which is the common mistake of just adding the two.

For three successive changes, apply the formula twice: combine the first two into a net%, then combine that result with the third change using the same formula again. This is invaluable in profit-loss chains, population growth-decline problems, and multi-step discount questions.

title: Puzzle Notation System
summary: Use a consistent shorthand — confirmed values, undecided pairs, and case branches — to track puzzle deductions without rereading the passage every time.
body:
Complex box, floor, and month puzzles become manageable once you adopt a **fixed notation** instead of rereading the passage every time.

**Core symbols:**
- A plain letter or number in a cell = **confirmed** placement.
- Two possible values written together, such as P/Q, = **possible, undecided**.
- A strikethrough or (x) next to a value = **eliminated** for that slot.
- A small superscript arrow (^) = a relative clue not yet fixed to an exact position, for example 'A lives above B' before floor numbers are known.

**Branching cases:** When a clue creates two genuine possibilities, for example 'D sits second to the left of E, who sits at an extreme end,' do not guess — open **Case 1** and **Case 2** as two mini-grids side by side, and carry every subsequent clue into both. Eliminate whichever case contradicts a later clue; the surviving case is your answer.

**Worked example:** Clue: 'Only one person sits between F and G, and G sits at one of the extreme ends.'
Open two cases: Case 1 = G at the left end, Case 2 = G at the right end. Apply the next clue (say, 'H sits immediately right of F') to both cases; only one will remain consistent by the third or fourth clue.

Always number your cases and recheck all earlier clues against the surviving case before finalizing — puzzles are lost more often to skipped reverification than to wrong deductions.

title: Syllogism Venn Shortcut
summary: Draw the minimum-overlap Venn diagram for each statement pair and apply the 'only a few' possibility rule to check conclusions in seconds.
body:
Skip formal rules and just **draw circles**. For two premises, draw the Venn diagram that satisfies both statements, then check if the conclusion is true in every possible diagram, not just one.

**The four basic relations:**
| Statement | Venn meaning |
|---|---|
| All A are B | A circle fully inside B circle |
| No A is B | A and B circles fully separate |
| Some A are B | A and B circles overlap partially |
| Some A are not B | Part of A is outside B |

**'Only a few' rule:** 'Only a few A are B' means: some A are B, and some A are not B — both parts must hold together, so draw a partial overlap where neither circle fully contains the other.

**Worked example:** All cats are dogs. Some dogs are birds.
Conclusion: 'Some cats are birds.'
Draw cats fully inside dogs. Now place the birds overlap with dogs — it can overlap dogs on the side away from cats. Since this alternate diagram is possible and breaks the conclusion, the conclusion does **not** follow.

**Possibility cases:** For conclusions using 'possibility' (for example, 'Some A can be C'), the conclusion holds true if there is at least one valid Venn diagram supporting it, even if other valid diagrams do not. This is the opposite test from definite conclusions, so always check whether the question is asking for a definite or a possibility conclusion before drawing.

title: Coded Inequality Decoding Table
summary: Build a decode table mapping each symbol to its meaning before combining statements, then apply the standard priority order to merge inequality chains.
body:
Coded inequality questions replace greater-than, less-than, and equal-to signs with symbols like @, #, $, %, and &. Before touching the statements, **build a decode table**:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| @ | greater than |
| # | less than |
| $ | equal to |
| % | greater than or equal to |
| & | less than or equal to |

Write this table at the top of your rough sheet so you never re-derive it midway.

**Combining chains:** Once decoded, treat the statement as a normal inequality chain and combine only when the direction is consistent. A > B >= C gives A > C, but A > B <= C tells you nothing about A versus C.

**Worked example:** Statements 'A @ B % C' and 'C # D' decode to A > B >= C and C < D.
Combining the first gives A > B >= C, so A > C.
C < D means D > C, but this does not chain with A > C, so the relation between A and D cannot be established.

**Priority for strict versus equal:** In a mixed chain, the end-to-end relation is strict only if every link in between is strict; if even one link carries 'or equal to,' the end relation must carry that possibility too.

title: Blood-Relation Symbol Notation
summary: Chart family relationships with plus/minus generation levels and gender-marked initials so multi-generation puzzles resolve into a simple family tree.
body:
Convert every blood-relation sentence into a **quick family-tree chart** instead of holding it in your head.

**Notation:**
- Draw a horizontal generation line; same generation sits on the same row.
- One row above = parent's generation (+1); one row below = child's generation (-1); two rows above = grandparent's generation (+2).
- Mark M or F next to each initial for gender once known.
- An '=' sign between two people on the same row means they are a married couple.
- A line down to the row below means a parent-child link.

**Worked example:** 'A is the son of B. B is the sister of C. C is the father of D.'
- Row +1: B and C, connected as siblings, with C marked M since C is D's father.
- Row 0: A (below B, since A is B's son) and D (below C, since D is C's child).
- So A and D sit on the same row as children of siblings, meaning A and D are cousins — no need to reread the sentences again.

**Reading questions fast:** Once the chart is built, 'how is A related to D' is answered by looking at the row difference and the path between them, rather than reparsing English sentences under time pressure. Always fix genders as soon as a pronoun or term such as son, daughter, or father reveals them, marking uncertain gender with a question mark until resolved.

title: Direction-Sense Grid Plotting Method
summary: Plot every movement on an imaginary compass grid with signed coordinates so the final displacement and direction are read off directly, not recalculated mentally.
body:
Never track direction problems in your head — **plot coordinates** on a simple grid, treating your starting point as the origin (0,0).

**Setup:** North adds to y, South subtracts from y, East adds to x, West subtracts from x. Every move updates your (x, y) position by the distance travelled in that direction.

**Worked example:** 'Ravi walks 5 km North, then 3 km East, then 5 km South, then 4 km East. Find his distance and direction from the start.'
- Start (0,0).
- 5 km North -> (0, 5).
- 3 km East -> (3, 5).
- 5 km South -> (3, 0).
- 4 km East -> (7, 0).

Final position (7, 0) is 7 km **East** of the start, since the North and South movements cancelled exactly. Distance = 7 km, direction = East.

**Reading final direction from coordinates:** Once you have the final (x, y), the direction is: both positive means North-East, x positive with y negative means South-East, x negative with y positive means North-West, and both negative means South-West. Use straight-line distance only if the question explicitly asks for shortest distance; otherwise report the simple value along the final axis of movement, as shown above.

**Common trap:** Watch for 'left turn' and 'right turn' instructions relative to the person's current facing direction, not fixed compass directions — update the facing direction at every turn before plotting the next move.

title: RC Strategy: Questions-First vs Passage-First
summary: Skim question stems before reading dense or unfamiliar passages, and eliminate extreme-language options first when answers require inference.
body:
Not every RC passage should be attacked the same way. Choose your approach based on passage type.

**Passage-first (read top to bottom fully):** Use this for narrative, opinion, or moderately easy editorial passages where flow matters — you will naturally retain the structure and tone, making inference questions faster to answer later.

**Questions-first (skim question stems, then read):** Use this for long, dense, unfamiliar-topic passages, such as economic or scientific reports, where you would otherwise reread multiple times. Skimming stems tells you what to hunt for, such as dates, contrasts, and named entities, so your one read-through stays targeted.

**Eliminating extreme options:** For inference and tone questions, options containing absolute words such as always, never, completely, only, and impossible are usually wrong unless the passage itself uses equally absolute language. Passages that hedge with words like may, often, and tends to rarely support extreme conclusions.

**Worked example:** A passage states that banking reforms 'have improved credit access for small businesses in many regions, though gaps remain in rural areas.' A question asks what the passage suggests.
Eliminate any option claiming reforms completely solved, or had no effect on, rural credit — both are extreme relative to the hedged original language. The correct option should mirror the passage's own qualified tone: partial improvement, with gaps remaining.

Combine both habits: pick your reading order by passage type, then apply the extreme-language filter to shortlist options before final selection.

title: Para-Jumble Anchor Technique
summary: Identify the opener sentence using standalone-idea cues, then chain the rest using pronoun and connector links rather than guessing a full order at once.
body:
Do not sequence all sentences at once — find the **anchor**, or opener, first, then build links one pair at a time.

**Finding the opener:**
- The opener introduces a subject in general terms; avoid pronouns (it, this, they, he, she), conjunctions (but, and, so), or a specific detail that assumes prior context.
- Prefer a sentence that names the subject fully, such as 'The Reserve Bank of India introduced a new framework,' over a vague reference like 'This framework.'

**Chaining the rest:**
- A sentence starting with 'this,' 'these,' 'it,' or 'they' must follow a sentence that introduces that exact noun.
- Connectors such as 'however,' 'therefore,' 'in addition,' and 'as a result' signal contrast, conclusion, addition, or consequence with the immediately preceding sentence.
- Repeated key nouns across two sentences often mark consecutive order.

**Worked example:** Four sentences: (P) 'This led to a sharp fall in bond yields.' (Q) 'The central bank cut its policy rate sharply.' (R) 'However, inflation expectations remained anchored.' (S) 'Analysts had widely expected this move.'
Q is the opener: it introduces the action fully with no pronoun. P follows Q, since 'this' refers to the rate cut, and R follows P via the contrast connector 'however.' Rereading confirms Q-S-P-R flows best, since S comments on the cut Q introduced, before P's consequence. Always reread the full assembled order once before finalizing — this last check catches ordering slips the pair-by-pair method misses.

title: Error-Spotting 10-Second Checklist
summary: Scan every sentence in a fixed order — subject-verb agreement, then tense, then preposition, then pronoun — to catch the error type fastest.
body:
Random reading wastes time; scan sentences in this **fixed priority order** every single time, since these four categories cause most errors.

**1. Subject-verb agreement:** Find the real subject, ignoring words between the subject and the verb, such as phrases beginning with 'along with,' 'as well as,' or 'together with.' Check that singular matches singular and plural matches plural.

**2. Tense:** Check consistency across the sentence, especially with 'since/for,' 'if' clauses, and reported speech; look for a verb tense that does not match the time markers given.

**3. Preposition:** Check fixed verb-preposition and adjective-preposition pairs, such as 'depend on,' 'married to,' 'different from,' and 'consist of' — these are frequently swapped for a similar-sounding wrong preposition.

**4. Pronoun:** Check number and gender agreement with its antecedent, and watch for ambiguous reference.

**Worked example:** 'The list of items, along with their prices, are printed on the last page.'
Step 1 catches it immediately: the real subject is 'list,' which is singular, not 'items' — the phrase 'along with their prices' is a non-essential insertion. The verb should be 'is,' not 'are.' There is no need to even check tense, preposition, or pronoun once subject-verb agreement already flags the error.

**Why this order:** Subject-verb agreement errors are the most frequent and fastest to spot, often visible in under five seconds; checking it first means many sentences resolve before you even reach the preposition or pronoun checks, saving overall time across the full set.

title: Cloze Flow Method
summary: Read the entire passage once before filling any blank, since each blank's answer depends on the passage's overall tone and logical flow, not just the local sentence.
body:
The single biggest mistake in cloze tests is filling each blank as soon as you reach it. Instead, follow three steps.

**Step 1 - Read the whole passage once, blanks and all,** without selecting any options. Note the overall tone, such as formal, critical, optimistic, or neutral, and the topic's direction, such as building an argument, describing a problem, or praising a policy.

**Step 2 - Fill the 'easy' blanks first**, meaning ones where grammar alone fixes the answer, such as when only one option fits the required preposition or verb form, regardless of the blank's position in the passage.

**Step 3 - Fill the remaining blanks using tone consistency.** The word chosen must match the passage's established tone, not just be grammatically valid in isolation.

**Worked example:** The tone from step 1 is clearly critical of a policy's implementation. A blank reads: 'The rollout, however, was ______ by delays and poor coordination.'
Options include 'marked,' 'celebrated,' 'accompanied,' 'preceded,' and 'rewarded.' Both 'marked' and 'accompanied' fit grammatically, but since the tone is critical and the sentence already signals a negative contrast with 'however' and 'delays,' 'marked' fits better as the stronger, more natural collocation with 'by delays.' 'Celebrated' and 'rewarded' clash with the critical tone entirely and are eliminated at step 1.

This top-down flow of whole passage, then easy blanks, then tone-matched blanks prevents the common trap of picking a word that fits its own sentence but contradicts the paragraph's overall direction two sentences later.

title: Root-Prefix-Suffix Vocabulary Building
summary: Learn eight high-yield word roots to decode the meaning of unfamiliar vocabulary in RC and vocabulary questions without memorizing word lists.
body:
Instead of memorizing thousands of isolated words, learn common **roots** — you can then decode dozens of unfamiliar words on sight.

**8 high-yield roots:**

| Root | Meaning | Example words |
|---|---|---|
| bene- | good, well | benefit, benevolent, benefactor |
| mal- | bad, wrong | malfunction, malice, malnutrition |
| chron- | time | chronological, synchronize, chronic |
| dict- | say, speak | predict, dictate, verdict |
| duc-/duct- | lead | conduct, induce, deduce |
| fract-/frag- | break | fracture, fragment, fragile |
| gen- | birth, origin | generate, genesis, congenital |
| port- | carry | transport, portable, export |

**How to use it:** When you meet an unfamiliar word in an RC passage or vocabulary question, break it into prefix, root, and suffix and estimate its meaning before checking the options.

**Worked example:** The word 'malediction' appears in a passage.
Break it down: 'mal-' (bad) plus 'dict' (say) gives literally 'a bad saying,' meaning a curse or a statement wishing harm. Even without ever having seen 'malediction' before, the roots alone get you to the correct meaning, letting you eliminate options like 'blessing' or 'compliment' immediately.

**Extending further:** Once a root is learned, actively spot it in new words during practice; after learning 'dict-,' notice it again in 'contradict,' 'edict,' and 'indict.' This compounds your effective vocabulary far faster than rote list memorization, and works even for words you have genuinely never encountered before.
